questions.title: How does exponential gating in sLSTM differ from standard sigmoid gating, and why is it necessary?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces exponential activation functions for the input gate (always) and optionally for the forget gate in sLSTM (Equation (5)). I understand that sigmoid gates output values in \([0,1]\) while the exponential can produce arbitrarily large numbers. How exactly does this change the dynamics of the cell update, and what problem does it solve that sigmoid gating cannot? Also, how does the normalizer state \(n_t\) prevent the exponential gates from causing numerical overflow?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the stabilizer state \(m_t\) in Equation (6), and how does it guarantee that the gradients remain unchanged?
questions.question_body: The authors define a stabilizer state \(m_t\) and then compute stabilized gates \(i'_t\) and \(f'_t\). They claim this does not alter the network output nor the loss gradients (Appendix A). Could someone walk through a concrete example or derivation showing why dividing by \(e^{m_t}\) leaves the forward and backward passes invariant?

questions.title: How is "memory mixing" implemented for sLSTM with multiple heads, and what does it mean that heads mix memory within but not across heads?
questions.question_body: The text says sLSTM can have multiple heads where mixing occurs only within each head. I am unclear on how the recurrent weight matrices \(\mathbf{R}_z,\mathbf{R}_i,\mathbf{R}_f,\mathbf{R}_o\) are applied when there are several heads. Does each head have its own set of these matrices, or is there a shared matrix that operates block‑diagonally? How does this arrangement affect the expressiveness compared to classic LSTM with a single vector memory?

questions.title: Why does the mLSTM use a matrix memory \(\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) rather than a vector, and how does the covariance update rule relate to Fast Weight Programmers?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2 the authors replace the scalar cell state with a matrix and update it with \(\mathbf{C}_t = f_t\mathbf{C}_{t-1}+ i_t\mathbf{v}_t\mathbf{k}_t^\top\). I would like to understand intuitively what storing a full matrix buys us in terms of capacity. Also, how is this update mathematically equivalent to a Fast Weight Programmer, and what role do the forget and input gates play as decay and learning rates respectively?

questions.title: How is the normalizer state \(\mathbf{n}_t\) defined for mLSTM, and why is a lower‑bound of 1 used in the denominator of \(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t\)?
questions.question_body: Equation (9) defines \(\mathbf{n}_t = f_t \mathbf{n}_{t-1}+ i_t \mathbf{k}_t\). Later the hidden state is computed as \(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t / \max\{|\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t|, 1\}\). Why is an absolute value taken, why is it compared to 1, and what would happen if we omitted this clipping? Is this analogous to normalization in attention mechanisms?

questions.title: What exactly are "pre up‑projection" and "post up‑projection" residual blocks, and why are they paired differently with mLSTM vs. sLSTM?
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 mentions two residual block designs: (i) post up‑projection (used with sLSTM) where non‑linear summarization happens before projecting to high dimension, and (ii) pre up‑projection (used with mLSTM) where projection happens first. Could someone illustrate these two architectures with a small diagram or pseudo‑code, and explain why the authors chose opposite orders for the two LSTM variants?

questions.title: In the synthetic formal‑language experiments, why do Transformers fail on tasks requiring state tracking while xLSTM succeeds?
questions.question_body: Figure 2 (referenced in the text) shows that models without memory mixing cannot solve parity‑type tasks. I want to understand theoretically why self‑attention lacks "state tracking" ability—does it stem from the absence of recurrent hidden‑to‑hidden connections? How does exponential gating plus memory mixing give xLSTM provable advantage on regular grammars like parity?

questions.title: How does the matrix memory size affect computational cost for mLSTM, and what are realistic limits on \(d\) for a 1B‑parameter model?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that mLSTM’s memory update involves \(d^2\) operations but is parallelizable. For a model with hidden dimension 4096, this seems huge. What proportion of total FLOPs comes from the matrix memory update versus standard linear layers? Are there heuristic guidelines for choosing \(d\) such that runtime stays comparable to a Transformer of similar parameter count?

questions.title: Can exponential gating lead to exploding gradients despite stabilization, and how should one initialize forget gate biases?
questions.question_body: Section 5 lists “initialization of forget gates must be chosen carefully” as a limitation. Given that \(f_t = \exp(\tilde f_t)\) can become very large, how does one set bias terms to avoid runaway growth early in training? Is there an recommended initialization scheme (e.g., bias=–1 for forget gate) that works specifically with exponential gating?

questions.title: What does the notation xLSTM[7:1] mean concretely in terms of block composition?
questions.question_body: The authors say xLSTM[7:1] means 7 out of 8 blocks are mLSTM‑based and 1 is sLSTM‑based. When stacking 48 blocks total, this translates to 42 mLSTM blocks and 6 sLSTM blocks. Are these blocks interleaved (e.g., every 8th block sLSTM), or placed consecutively? Does block order influence performance, and has any ablation been done on different arrangements?
